newsitem.title: USA: Northwest says safety allegations unfair.
newsitem.headline: Northwest says safety allegations unfair.

text.p: Northwest Airlines Corp on Thursday said accusations that its aircraft maintenance operations in Japan had problems were unfair.
"I think it's very unfair if someone's trying to paint a picture of Northwest not being a safe airline," Doug Killien, Northwest's director of international communications, said.

He was responding to a report in Japanese daily Asahi Shimbun that Japanese authorities had raised concerns with U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Northwest's maintenance operations in Japan, citing the carrier's high rate of incidents, such as emergency landings.
The newspaper said Northwest accounted for 20 of the 51 incidents, or 40 percent, that occurred on scheduled flights at Tokyo's Narita international airport in 1996.
It added that 21 of 205 such incidents across the country involved Northwest, which had an incident rate of one in every 800 flights, more than double the average.

"Of those 20 incidents that the airport authorities in Narita cites for Northwest in 1996, some were as minor as a plugged lavatory drain, which we elected to go back to Narita for," Killien said from the company's Minneapolis headquarters.

"Under FAA regulations for U.S. carriers, anytime we make a precautionary engine shutdown or decide to return, we need to declare an emergency," he said. "That is not the case for Japanese airlines, necessarily."
"We have a large maintenance base in Tokyo Narita airport, and if there is ever any irregularity in a flight, we will go back to Narita because it's a very large maintenance base," he added.
Killien said Northwest had not, to his knowledge, replaced managers in charge of maintenance in Japan as Asahi Shimbun had reported.
